submitted.rationale: Highest measured photocurrent (7e-8 A) at 2.06 eV illumination. Index 88 (Bi 0.35, Fe 0.23, V 0.42) is an Fe-alloyed composition close to BiVO4 stoichiometry. Photocurrent rose going from the Fe-V-rich index 0 to the Bi-V-rich index 30 and again to index 88, which has a Bi:V ratio closer to 1 and more Fe.

rejected.reason: Measured 6e-8 A, below index 88; V-rich relative to BiVO4 stoichiometry.
Measured 2e-8 A; the Fe-V-rich region was the weakest of the three despite expected absorption at 602 nm.

consultations.verdict: Uninformative-to-mild support: MEGNet HSE gap for Fe2O3 (mp-19770) is 2.77 eV, above the 2.06 eV photon energy, so the model can't say whether Fe-rich regions absorb. Index 30 sits at Bi:V ~1:1.5 with ~17% Fe, i.e. the Fe-alloyed BiVO4 region, which is the best-known photoanode chemistry here. I'm measuring it as the first anchor.

Mostly uninformative. Phase mp-504509 (I believe it is an Fe/V oxide, but I haven't checked its identity) has a predicted HSE gap of 2.75 eV. MEGNet overestimates the gaps of Fe-containing oxides; the Fe2O3 prediction of 2.77 eV is far above its roughly 2.1 eV experimental gap. Experimentally, Fe-V oxides absorb near 2.0-2.1 eV, so index 0 (Fe 0.44, V 0.43, low Bi) is the region most likely to absorb 602 nm light. I'm measuring it to contrast with the BiVO4-like anchor.

Uninformative for choosing a composition: MACE puts Fe2O3 (mp-19770) on the hull, which fits Fe segregating as hematite. That would add sub-2.1 eV absorption, but it doesn't rank the candidates. The measured data points the choice: the Bi-V-rich index 30 (6e-8 A) beat the Fe-V-rich index 0 (2e-8 A). Index 88 is closer to BiVO4 stoichiometry (Bi/V 0.82) and has more Fe (0.23), and it is in the GP top 5. I'm measuring it.
